title: Advances in targeting the FGF-FGFR Pathway to overcome acquired EGFR-TKI resistance in non-small cell lung cancer.
authors: Ding C, Luo Y, Lei Y et al.
abstract: Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remains a major cause of cancer-related mortality, and activating epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) mutations define a clinically important molecular subtype. EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) have substantially improved outcomes, but acquired resistance eventually limits long-term disease control. Among diverse resistance mechanisms, fibroblast growth factor receptor (FGFR) signaling has emerged as one of several potential bypass pathways. This review summarizes evidence implicating fibroblast growth factors (FGFs) and FGFRs in selected contexts of resistance to EGFR inhibition. Genetic alterations, including receptor fusions, amplifications, and activating mutations, and non-genetic mechanisms such as receptor overexpression and ligand-driven autocrine signaling may sustain downstream pathway activation. These processes can reactivate mitogenic and survival signaling despite EGFR inhibition and may support tumor persistence in a subset of molecular settings. We discuss preclinical and clinical evidence for FGFR-associated resistance, with particular emphasis on the functionally characterized FGF2-FGFR1 axis. Emerging therapeutic strategies, including selective FGFR inhibitors, multi-kinase inhibitors, and investigational combination regimens with EGFR inhibitors or immunotherapy, are reviewed with attention to current limitations. Finally, we highlight challenges related to biomarker identification, routine testing, toxicity management, and clinical trial design, and outline future directions for evaluating FGFR-targeted approaches in EGFR-mutant NSCLC.

title: Evolving treatment selection for advanced NSCLC with uncommon EGFR mutations: from mutation-based therapy to broader EGFR-directed strategies.
authors: Nagano Y

title: Molecular Discordance Between Primary Non-Small Cell Lung Cancers and Brain Metastases: Associations With Intracranial Outcomes.
authors: Jani JA, Hicks WH, Ma T et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: In an era of molecular-guided systemic oncologic therapies, a proportion of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) brain metastases (BMs) have demonstrated molecularly discordant profiles for anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK), epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), and Kirsten rat sarcoma viral oncogene homolog (KRAS) biomarkers compared with the primary tumor. However, its effect on outcomes remains unclear. We investigated the association between molecular discordance for these actionable markers and clinical outcomes in patients with NSCLC BM.
METHODS: We performed a single-institution retrospective analysis screening 476 patients who underwent treatment for a NSCLC BM from January 2012 to December 2025, with 40 patients having molecular profiling for the primary lung and BM lesions. Patient molecular profiles were categorized as concordant or discordant based on comparison of the ALK, EGFR, and KRAS mutational statuses at both tumor sites. Descriptive statistics, univariate comparisons, Kaplan-Meier survival, and Fine-Gray competing risk analyses were performed between the concordant and discordant cohorts. Multiple comparison using false discovery rate was performed for survival-related outcomes.
RESULTS: ALK, EGFR, or KRAS molecular discordance occurred in 32.5% (13/40) of observed cases. Although nonsignificant, the concordant cohort had a higher rate of distant brain failure (DBF) (63.0% vs 30.8%, P = .056); conversely, the discordant cohort had a higher rate of local recurrence (38.5% vs 18.5%, P = .17). The discordant cohort had a lower subdistribution hazard of DBF than the concordant cohort (subdistribution hazard ratio: 0.34, 95% CI: 0.13-0.91, P = .032). However, this significant difference did not persist after false discovery rate-adjusted analysis. Significant differences in time to intracranial progression, time to local recurrence, and overall survival were not observed between the 2 cohorts.
CONCLUSION: Molecular discordance was observed in >30% of analyzed cases, and the subdistribution hazard of DBF differed significantly between the 2 cohorts. This rate of discordance may warrant further investigation on whether increased BM profiling could help refine current approaches to NSCLC BM management.

title: Targeting Oncogenic EGFR and KRAS at the RNA Level: Emerging CRISPR-Cas13 and ADAR Strategies for Lung Adenocarcinoma.
authors: Singh DD
abstract: Lung adenocarcinoma remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide, with its development and progression frequently driven by oncogenic alterations in EGFR and KRAS. Although molecularly targeted therapies, particularly Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitors (TKIs), have substantially improved clinical outcomes in selected patients, their long-term efficacy is frequently compromised by acquired resistance, tumor heterogeneity, and mutation-specific differences in therapeutic response. These limitations underscore the need for alternative strategies capable of selectively targeting oncogenic drivers while minimizing irreversible genomic alterations. RNA-targeted therapeutics have emerged as a potential therapeutic approach because they enable transient, programmable, and potentially reversible modulation of disease-associated transcripts without permanently modifying genomic DNA. Among these technologies, CRISPR-Cas13 and Adenosine Deaminase Acting on RNA (ADAR)-based editing systems offer distinct yet complementary mechanisms for manipulating oncogenic RNA. Cas13 enables sequence-specific recognition, degradation, or modulation of target transcripts, whereas engineered ADAR platforms facilitate site-directed Adenosine-to-Inosine (A-to-I) editing, allowing precise correction or functional recoding of selected RNA sequences. These approaches provide opportunities to selectively target clinically relevant mutant transcripts, including KRAS G12D/G12V and resistance-associated EGFR variants, while preserving their wild-type counterparts. Furthermore, Cas13-ADAR-based platforms may combine programmable RNA recognition with nucleotide-level editing to enhance specificity and expand the range of therapeutic applications. Emerging evidence from cancer cell lines, patient-derived organoids, and animal models supports the feasibility of programmable RNA targeting; however, efficient tumor-specific delivery, off-target and collateral effects, immunogenicity, editing efficiency, and durability remain major barriers to clinical translation. Compared with permanent DNA editing, RNA editing offers potential advantages in reversibility, controllability, and reduced risk of persistent genomic off-target alterations. This review examines the molecular basis of EGFR- and KRAS-driven lung adenocarcinoma; recent advances in Cas13- and ADAR-mediated RNA targeting; delivery strategies; safety considerations; and preclinical progress, while highlighting the key challenges and future directions required to translate programmable RNA editing into precision therapies for lung adenocarcinoma.

title: The evolving immune ecosystem of TKI resistance in EGFR-mutant NSCLC: from treatment-induced remodeling to mechanism-guided therapy.
authors: Luo B, Hairulajiang A, Liu J et al.
abstract: Tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) have transformed the treatment of EGFR-mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), yet acquired resistance remains a major clinical limitation. Resistance is increasingly understood as an evolving state shaped not only by tumor-cell genomic alterations but also by treatment-induced remodeling of the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME). This Review examines how EGFR-TKI exposure reshapes macrophage states, T-cell function and localization, fibroblast and myeloid niches, and vascular architecture, and how these changes are reinforced by immune-checkpoint adaptation, metabolic reprogramming, and phenotypic plasticity. We then connect the evolving TIME to post-TKI therapeutic strategies according to the maturity of the supporting evidence, including immune checkpoint inhibitor-containing regimens, anti-angiogenic combinations, mechanism-matched targeted therapy, antibody-drug conjugates, bispecific T-cell engagers, and selected preclinical microenvironment-directed approaches. Finally, we discuss circulating biomarkers, single-cell sequencing, and spatial profiling as tools for longitudinally defining resistant immune states. Viewing TKI resistance as a temporally evolving immune ecosystem provides a framework for linking resistance mechanism, immune phenotype, and treatment selection rather than treating progression as a purely genomic endpoint.

title: High-dose administration of EGFR-TKIs for NSCLC patients: a literature review.
authors: Cheng K, Chen Y, Tao X et al.
abstract: High-dose EGFR-TKIs have been used as an exploratory therapeutic strategy to overcome the limitations of the standard-dose regimen in the treatment of EGFR-mutant NSCLC, particularly in patients with CNS metastases. Available clinical evidence suggests that high-dose TKIs confer certain therapeutic efficacy and manageable safety profiles, with a small proportion of patients experiencing ≥3 grade adverse events, such as rash, nausea,diarrhea, aminotransferase rise, leukopenia.However, the evidence is limited by the predominance of single-center retrospective studies, small sample sizes, heterogeneous patient populations and short follow-up periods. Further large-scale, multicenter studies with long-term follow-up are needed to define more clearly the efficacy, safety, and appropriate clinical role of high-dose EGFR-TKI therapy.

title: Integration of bulk and single-cell transcriptomics via the Scissor algorithm reveals APOE-dependent cholesterol metabolic reprogramming in macrophages associated with osimertinib resistance in non-small cell lung cancer.
authors: Gong Z, Gao Z, Zhang J et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The tumor microenvironment contributes to acquired resistance against osimertinib in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), yet the key cell subpopulations and the underlying metabolic mechanisms remain incompletely elucidated.
METHODS: The Scissor algorithm was applied to integrate bulk osimertinib-resistance transcriptomic profiles with single-cell RNA-seq data to pinpoint cell subpopulations functionally associated with the osimertinib resistant phenotype. AddModuleScore was applied to calculate scores for cholesterol metabolism-related modules. Gene-set enrichment analysis was carried out to uncover pathway alterations in osimertinib resistance-related macrophages. Cross-validation was performed in an independent dataset comparing treatment-naive and EGFR-tyrosine kinase inhibitors (EGFR-TKIs)-treated progressive-disease lesions. EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinoma cells were treated with corresponding conditioned medium combined with osimertinib, followed by a panel of cell function assays, including cell proliferation, colony formation, and apoptosis. The gain- and loss- of function studies of APOE were conducted in THP-1 derived macrophages.
RESULTS: Osimertinib-resistant associated Scissor+ cells were mainly enriched within macrophages, which exhibited prominent APOE-dependent cholesterol metabolic reprogramming. APOE was markedly up-regulated in Scissor+ macrophages and macrophages from EGFR-TKI-treated progressive-disease lesions. Macrophage-derived APOE shapes extracellular cholesterol availability in the microenvironment, which may promote intracellular free-cholesterol accumulation in tumor cells and counteract osimertinib-triggered apoptosis.
CONCLUSION: APOE-dependent cholesterol metabolic reprogramming in macrophages is associated with osimertinib resistance in NSCLC and may contribute to therapeutic failure. Our results identify APOE as a hypothesis-generating candidate molecule that merits further pre-clinical investigation.

title: Metastatic lung adenocarcinoma harboring an ERBB2 exon 20 insertion and low-level copy-number gain: hyperprogression after immunotherapy and sequential HER2-directed ADC therapy-a case report.
authors: Xia X, Liu L, Du W
abstract:
BACKGROUND: HER2 (ERBB2) alterations in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) comprise a molecularly heterogeneous group, including activating mutations, copy-number gain/amplification, and protein overexpression. HER2 mutation and high-level amplification are generally distinct biological events. HER2-directed antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) have transformed treatment, yet questions remain regarding sequencing, coexisting HER2 alterations, and central nervous system (CNS) progression.
CASE DESCRIPTION: A never-smoking woman presented in August 2025 with stage IVB (T4N3M1c2, AJCC v9) right upper-lobe lung adenocarcinoma with nodal, brain, renal, bone, adrenal, and abdominal/retroperitoneal metastases (ECOG 1-2). A 919-gene NGS panel identified an ERBB2 exon 20 insertion, p.Y772_A775dup (VAF 58.4%), with low-level ERBB2 copy-number gain (copy number 3.1); TP53 p.I195T and p.R249S were also detected. PD-L1 tumor proportion score (TPS) was 40%. Because of symptomatic, high-volume disease, cycle 1 (August 31, 2025) consisted of pemetrexed plus carboplatin before biomarker results were available; ivonescimab was added in cycle 2 (September 23, 2025). Restaging on October 15, 2025 showed marked multi-compartment progression: the lung target lesion increased from 4.56 cm to 10.05 cm (>120%), with new brain, renal, and adrenal metastases, retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy, a large right pleural effusion, and deterioration to ECOG 3-4, consistent with hyperprogressive disease (HPD), which was temporally associated with immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) exposure-occurring approximately 3 weeks after the first, and only, dose of ivonescimab and without disease acceleration during the preceding chemotherapy-only cycle. Trastuzumab rezetecan was initiated on October 16, 2025 for six cycles. By December 5, 2025, the lung lesion had shrunk to 5.68 cm with reduced pleural effusion and partial intracranial improvement; best overall response was partial response (PR). Restaging on March 1, 2026 demonstrated spatially heterogeneous progression: thoracic disease and pleural effusion remained controlled, whereas renal, adrenal, retroperitoneal nodal, skeletal, and intracranial lesions progressed, with meningeal enhancement suspicious for leptomeningeal metastasis (lumbar puncture declined). No cranial radiotherapy or surgery was ever administered. Progression-free survival (PFS) was approximately 4.5 months and duration of response (DOR) approximately 2.9 months. Zongertinib 120 mg once daily was started on March 2, 2026, but was discontinued after 7 days because of financial constraints, precluding objective response assessment. The patient died on May 15, 2026, with an overall survival (OS) of approximately 9.5 months.
CONCLUSION: In this case of metastatic lung adenocarcinoma with a concurrent ERBB2 exon 20 insertion and low-level copy-number gain, urgent biomarker-agnostic chemo-immunotherapy was followed by HPD after a single ivonescimab cycle, whereas molecularly matched trastuzumab rezetecan produced a rapid partial response with systemic and transient intracranial control before spatially heterogeneous progression emerged. Salvage zongertinib was clinically rational but could not be objectively assessed because of limited exposure. This case highlights how biomarker turnaround time, drug accessibility, and compartment-specific resistance shape the real-world management of HER2-driven NSCLC, and emphasizes the diagnosis of HPD and its temporal association with ICI exposure. The case also has implications for patient selection, supporting early molecular characterization and the prioritization of molecularly matched HER2-directed therapy in patients with actionable oncogenic drivers.

title: MiRNA-1915-3p dysregulation characterizes aggressive CRBP1-expressing lung adenocarcinoma cells in vitro and in patient-derived tissues.
authors: Ferlosio A, Centofanti F, Doldo E et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) is the most common histological subtype and a leading cause of cancer mortality worldwide. Cellular Retinol Binding Protein-1 (CRBP1) regulates intracellular retinol bioavailability and several transcriptional activities in normal and neoplastic cells. High CRBP1 expression in LUAD has been previously shown to correlate with worse tumor grade and prognosis. We therefore investigated the putative mechanisms through which CRBP1 expression influences LUAD progression.
METHODS: We analyzed genomic copy number variations, miRNA and gene expression, as well as protein levels and ubiquitination status in CRBP1-transfected A549 cells and in CRBP1-expressing LUAD tissues.
RESULTS: Bioinformatics analysis revealed that high expression of CRBP1 in both transfected A549 cells and LUAD tissues is associated with miR-1915-3p downregulation. In silico analysis of the interactions between deregulated miR-1915-3p and gene expression identified EGFR and RARα as potential targets. Consistently, western blot analysis confirmed EGFR and RARα upregulation in CRBP1-transfected A549 cells. However, CRBP1-induced EGFR upregulation occurred independently of proteasomal degradation, as no changes in EGFR ubiquitination or protein stability were observed after MG132 treatment. Finally, pathway enrichment analysis revealed that CRBP1 expression is related to the modulation of several genes belonging to cancer pathways.
CONCLUSIONS: Our findings identify a CRBP1-driven molecular landscape characterized by miR-1915-3p suppression and EGFR/RARα upregulation, providing a new hypothetical framework for understanding potential mechanisms of LUAD progression, which requires further validation in larger cohorts.

title: Survival of Lung Cancer Patients With Private or Statutory Health Insurance: An Evaluation of Data From the CRISP Registry (AIO-TRK-0315) on Patients With Advanced Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer.
authors: Acker F, Thomas M, Eberhardt WEE et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: In some health systems, insurance status can have a major effect on the quality of treatment that cancer patients receive and on their chances of survival; hardly any data on this matter are available for Germany. In this study, indicators of treatment quality and survival were compared among patients with advanced or metastatic non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) who were covered by either private or statutory health insurance (PHI or SHI, respectively).
METHODS: Patients whose data were included in CRISP, a national prospective lung cancer registry for Germany, between 2016 and 2023 were compared using propensity score matching according to their health insurance status, in a 1:1 ratio.
RESULTS: 924 of the 8646 patients included in CRISP over the study period were privately insured. The overall survival of patients with PHI and SHI in the matched cohort (1848 patients total) was comparable (hazard ratio 1.01, 95% confidence interval [0.90; 1.13]); nor was there any difference with respect to survival in the subgroups of patients who were initially treated with immunotherapy, chemotherapy alone, or epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) inhibitors. The median time from diagnosis to the start of treatment in patients in the matched cohort was 4.4 weeks (interquartile range 2.6-6.6 weeks) for those with SHI and 4.0 weeks (2.6-6.1 weeks) for those with PHI. Independently of their insurance status, 77.3% of patients in 2023 underwent a determination of treatment-relevant biomarkers in conformity with the relevant guidelines.
CONCLUSION: No relevant differences depending on insurance status were found in the quality indicators studied or in the overall survival of patients with advanced or metastatic NSCLC. In view of the trans-sectoral recruitment of patients for the CRISP registry, these findings would appear to be generalizable to Germany as a whole.

title: Efficacy and safety of third-generation EGFR-TKIs combined with local consolidative therapy as first-line treatment for EGFR-mutated stage IIIB-IV NSCLC: a retrospective study.
authors: Zhang Z, Qiao D, Sun Z et al.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Although third-generation EGFR-tyrosine kinase inhibitors (EGFR-TKIs), such as osimertinib and aumolertinib, can improve prognosis as first-line treatment, most patients inevitably develop resistance and disease progression (PD). Local consolidative therapy (LCT) combined with TKIs can enhance therapeutic efficacy, but the existing evidence is mainly based on first- and second-generation TKIs. This retrospective case-control study aimed to evaluate whether the combination of LCT with third-generation EGFR-TKIs treatment can improve the efficacy and safety in the management of advanced NSCLC compared with TKIs monotherapy.
METHODS: This retrospective study enrolled patients diagnosed with EGFR-mutant NSCLC. The experimental group received EGFR-TKIs combined with LCT, and the control group received EGFR-TKIs monotherapy. The primary endpoints were progression-free survival (PFS) and duration of objective response (DOR), which were compared using the Kaplan‑Meier method and log‑rank test; hazard ratios (HR) were analyzed by the Cox proportional hazards model. Subgroup analyses were conducted to investigate the heterogeneity. The patterns of PD and adverse events were summarized.
RESULTS: A total of 49 patients were enrolled in this study (combination therapy group: n = 27; monotherapy group: n = 22). The median PFS was significantly longer in the combination therapy group than in the monotherapy group (32.0 vs. 21.0 months; HR = 0.39, P = 0.012). The DOR was also superior in the combination therapy group (29.0 vs. 17.0 months; HR = 0.36, 95% CI: 0.16-0.78, P = 0.006). Subgroup analyses showed that significant PFS benefit from combination therapy can be observed in patients with extrathoracic metastasis and those who achieved partial response after TKI treatment. Multivariate Cox regression analysis identified combination local therapy (HR = 0.29, 95% CI: 0.12-0.70) and ≤ 5 metastatic lesions (HR = 0.12, 95% CI: 0.02-0.56) as independent prognostic factors for PFS. Analysis of disease progression patterns revealed that 87.5% of progression events in the combination therapy group occurred at sites not treated with LCT, while 80% of progression events in the monotherapy group arose from baseline pre-existing lesions. No statistically significant difference was found in the incidence of grade 1-2 and grade 3 adverse events between the two groups (all P > 0.05).
CONCLUSION: Third-generation EGFR-TKIs combined with LCT can significantly prolong PFS and DOR in patients with advanced EGFR-mutant NSCLC, with manageable safety.

title: Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor-producing lung squamous cell carcinoma positive for an uncommon EGFR Exon 20 S768I mutation: a case report.
authors: Inadomi Y, Sawai T, Gyotoku H et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) lung carcinoma is a rare and highly aggressive clinical entity characterized by persistent neutrophilia, high fever, and poor prognosis. Although the lung is a common primary site, the co-occurrence of G-CSF production and epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) mutations is extremely rare, particularly in squamous cell carcinoma (SCC).
CASE PRESENTATION: A 79-year-old Asian man, a former smoker, presented with an 80 mm mass in the left upper lobe and was diagnosed with a G-CSF-producing lung SCC (cT4N2bM0, cStage IIIB). Genetic testing identified a minor mutation and high programmed death ligand 1 (PD-L1) expression (tumor proportion score: TPS 65%). Despite an initial partial response to concurrent chemoradiotherapy, the disease progressed rapidly during maintenance durvalumab therapy, with a marked secondary increase in serum G-CSF and interleukin 6 (IL-6) levels. Subsequent lines of therapy, including docetaxel and the EGFR-tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) afatinib and osimertinib, provided only transient or limited clinical benefits. The patient eventually succumbed to tumor progression 22 months after the initial diagnosis.
DISCUSSION: To the best of our knowledge, this is the first English-language report of a G-CSF-producing lung SCC harboring an EGFR S768I mutation. The present findings suggest that the inflammatory and immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment associated with G-CSF and IL-6 production may contribute to resistance against both immune checkpoint inhibitors and EGFR-TKIs, even when targetable mutations are present.
CONCLUSION: Although driver mutations are rare in G-CSF-producing lung carcinoma, their presence may not guarantee a good response to targeted therapies. This case underscores the need for careful treatment selection and highlights the importance of further research into the mechanisms of treatment resistance in this intractable phenotype.

title: Therapeutic resistance in brain malignancies: mechanisms limiting drug efficacy and emerging pharmacological strategies.
authors: Chen L, Zhang N, He M et al.
abstract: Therapeutic resistance in malignant brain tumors does not arise from a single molecular abnormality, but rather from the interplay among insufficient drug exposure, intrinsic and adaptive tumor-cell dependencies, cell-state plasticity, and the intracranial microenvironment. Although central nervous system (CNS)-active tyrosine kinase inhibitors, human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2)-targeted antibody-drug conjugates, and immune checkpoint inhibitors have improved intracranial outcomes in selected patients with brain metastases harboring actionable molecular alterations or immunologically responsive features, many mechanistically compelling strategies for glioblastoma (GBM) have yet to translate consistently into survival benefits in randomized clinical trials beyond the current standard of care. Rather than equating an association with resistance with therapeutic actionability, this Review evaluates resistance mechanisms and their potential for intervention through five linked steps: whether a drug can achieve sufficient exposure within intracranial lesions and critical resistance niches; whether the intervention produces sustained target modulation or the intended pharmacodynamic effect; whether the implicated mechanism represents a causal driver of resistance or an actionable dependency rather than merely a descriptive correlate; whether the therapeutic window permits repeated treatment at clinically relevant doses and schedules; and whether intervention yields reproducible intracranial responses, durable disease control, or survival benefit. Reproducible predictive and pharmacodynamic biomarkers support patient selection and assessment across these steps. Within this framework, we compare the distinct pharmacological and clinical implications of the blood-brain barrier/blood-tumor barrier, DNA damage response, cancer stem-like cell states, and immune evasion in GBM and brain metastases from lung cancer, breast cancer, and melanoma. We further examine the pharmacological rationale, maturity of evidence, and practical limitations of emerging approaches, including drug repurposing, antibody-drug conjugates, synthetic-lethal strategies, microenvironmental reprogramming, and rational combination therapies. Future progress will depend less on expanding the catalogue of resistance mechanisms than on embedding spatial pharmacokinetics, longitudinal molecular monitoring, and functional validation into clinical trials, thereby enabling mechanistic insights into resistance to be translated into specific, testable, and dynamically adaptable therapeutic decisions.

title: Conversion Surgery After EGFR-TKI Induction for Initially Unresectable EGFR-Mutant Stage III NSCLC.
authors: Jiang Y, Lin Y, Chen P et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Patients with stage III epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) may be considered unresectable because of mediastinal nodal disease or invasion of adjacent structures. We evaluated whether EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (EGFR-TKI)-based induction therapy could enable conversion surgery in selected patients with initially unresectable disease.
PATIENTS AND METHODS: We retrospectively identified 162 consecutive patients with initially unresectable stage IIIA-N2b to IIIC EGFR-mutant NSCLC who received EGFR-TKI-based induction therapy between January 2017 and December 2022. After induction, 70 patients were considered technically resectable by multidisciplinary reassessment. Of these, 42 chose conversion surgery and 28 declined surgery and continued non-surgical treatment. Perioperative outcomes, pathologic response, downstaging, event-free survival (EFS), and overall survival (OS) were evaluated. Inverse probability of treatment weighting was used to reduce measured confounding.
RESULTS: All 42 surgical patients underwent video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery without conversion to thoracotomy. R0 resection was achieved in 41 patients (97.6%). Major pathologic response was observed in 13 patients (31.0%), including 1 patient (2.4%) with pathologic complete response. Lymph-node downstaging occurred in 25 patients (59.5%). After weighting, conversion surgery was associated with longer EFS and OS than non-surgical treatment.
CONCLUSION: In this selected retrospective cohort, conversion surgery after EGFR-TKI-based induction was feasible and was associated with longer EFS and OS than continued non-surgical treatment. This investigational strategy requires prospective validation before routine use.

title: A Study of SKB571 Combined With SKB118 ± Chemotherapy in Locally Advanced or Metastatic NSCLC
summary: This is an open-label, multicenter, Phase II clinical study to evaluate the safety, tolerability, and efficacy of SKB571 in combination with SKB118 ± chemotherapy in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC ) participants.

title: Transcription factor subtype governs response and resistance to DLL3-directed T cell engagement in small cell lung cancer.
authors: Vasseur D, Saito S, Gulati GS et al.
abstract: Although small cell lung cancer (SCLC) comprises transcription factor (TF)-defined molecular subtypes (ASCL1, NEUROD1, and POU2F3), whether these predict therapeutic response or evolve under therapeutic pressure remains unclear. Tarlatamab, a DLL3 × CD3 bispecific T cell engager, has transformed SCLC therapy, yet responses are heterogeneous and resistance develops in most patients. We inferred tumor gene expression from circulating chromatin in patient plasma and developed an immunocompetent syngeneic mouse model to study tarlatamab response and resistance. Across patients and mice, TF subtypes associated with response or resistance. ASCL1 tumors were enriched for response, consistent with DLL3 being an ASCL1 target gene, while NEUROD1 tumors had inferior responses and POU2F3 tumors were intrinsically resistant. Acquired resistance involved selection for a NEUROD1-high state with downregulation of the ASCL1-linked antigen DLL3 or enrichment of regulatory and exhausted T cell programs. These findings support TF-defined subtypes as clinically relevant frameworks for understanding tarlatamab response and resistance in SCLC.

title: RCT of SBRT for oligometastatic NSCLC.
authors: Lin TC, Liao CY, Chien CR
abstract: We read with great interest the systematic review recently published in Clinical and Experimental Metastasis (Clin Exp Metastasis. 2026;43(6):62), which synthesized the evidence including two randomized controlled trials (RCTs).Given the central role of RCTs in establishing high-level evidence within evidence-based medicine, we write to highlight one omitted RCT as well as a recently published RCT relevant to this topic. We believe incorporating these studies complements the findings of the systematic review and provides readers with a more comprehensive overview of the current randomized evidence supporting stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) in oligometastatic non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC).

title: Mobilizing Collective Work Across Stakeholder Groups and Practice Settings to Normalize Guideline-Based LDCT Lung Cancer Screening Processes in U.S. Primary Care.
authors: Ezenwankwo E, Jones C, Barta JA et al.
abstract: This article, the second in a two-paper integrative review, synthesizes evidence on the mechanisms underpinning the collective work required to normalize and sustain guideline-recommended lung cancer screening (LCS) processes in U.S. primary care and the outcomes of those efforts. Seven electronic databases were searched through December 2025 to identify relevant primary studies. Evidence from 175 studies was integrated using thematic synthesis. Four themes capture mechanisms underpinning collective work: 1) building a shared understanding of LCS; 2) collective ownership of LCS work in routine practice; 3) enacting and integrating LCS processes into clinical workflows; and 4) evaluating and adapting LCS practices over time. Three themes capture outcomes of normalization efforts: 1) accessibility and routine activation of LCS processes in primary care; 2) guideline concordance in LCS delivery; and 3) redefining roles, relationships, and accountability for LCS. Collective work toward normalization often required stakeholders to make sense of LCS as fundamentally distinct from other cancer screenings. Across settings, opportunities emerge as stakeholders build shared understanding, secure buy-in, collectively organize, take ownership of, and enact LCS work despite contextual constraints, and continuously evaluate/adapt screening processes. However, important gaps persist, including in provider knowledge and confidence regarding the evidence supporting LDCT. Many providers lacked confidence in LDCT effectiveness or the ability to apply guideline recommendations consistently, contributing to substantial variation in recommendations and practices. More broadly, normalization requires expanding roles and training across the primary care team, along with system-level and structural support beyond what is typically required for established cancer screening programs.

title: Early detection of lung cancer: The past, present, and future.
authors: Leung B, Johnston S, Myers R et al.
abstract: Lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer-related deaths in Canada, primarily due to late-stage diagnoses. While the 5-year survival rate is 69%-82% for stage I disease, it drops sharply to 21%-44% for stage III, and 7%-18% for stage IV. To address this public health crisis, this review examines the evolution and implementation of Canadian lung cancer screening programs. Landmark clinical trials, including the National Lung Screening Trial (NLST) and the Dutch-Belgian lung cancer screening trial (Nederlands-Leuvens Longkanker Screenings Onderzoek [NELSON]) have unequivocally demonstrated that screening with low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) significantly reduces mortality. Presently, all 10 Canadian provinces are advancing organized screening programs utilizing the PLCOm2012 risk prediction model. However, significant systemic gaps persist. Current eligibility criteria rely heavily on smoking history, inadvertently excluding individuals who have never smoked-a demographic accounting for nearly one-quarter of all lung cancer cases. This exclusion disproportionately affects women of South and East Asian descent. Furthermore, geographic barriers limit access for isolated rural populations, and current screening guidelines lack consensus regarding survivors of non-pulmonary primary cancers. To mitigate these limitations, this review explores emerging early detection modalities, including the systematic management of incidental pulmonary nodules, breathomics, and artificial intelligence. Finally, it emphasizes the pivotal role of oncology nurses in patient advocacy, radon education, and tobacco cessation to maximize screening efficacy and ensure equitable access for all Canadians.

title: Cytokeratin 19 role in malignancy: a systematic review.
authors: Shahshenas S, Yarmohammadi H, Soltanipur M et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cytokeratin 19 (CK19) has emerged as an important biomarker in epithelial malignancies. Its expression is closely linked to cellular differentiation, tumor aggressiveness, and metastatic potential. This systematic review aimed to comprehensively evaluate CK19 expression across human malignant cell lines and assess its potential diagnostic, prognostic, and therapeutic implications.
METHODS: A systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science up to September 2024. Using a combination of MeSH terms and keywords "Cytokeratin 19", "Cell line", "Cell culture"), studies reporting CK19 expression in human malignant cell lines were identified. Only English-language publications were included. Data from the included articles were extracted and tabulated.
RESULTS: A total of 3205 articles were initially identified, with 264 studies ultimately meeting the inclusion criteria after duplicate and irrelevant publication removal. These studies evaluated CK19 expression across 476 human malignant cell lines from 32 different cancer types. In epithelial-derived tumors, notably breast, liver, and colorectal cancers, cell lines such as MCF-7, T47D, and SKBR3 consistently demonstrated high CK19 positivity, whereas MDA-MB-231 and other lines exhibited variable expression. In contrast, several lung cancer cell lines and specific non-epithelial models displayed low or absent CK19 levels. The analysis also revealed that CK19 expression is modulated by various treatments: chemotherapeutic agents, epigenetic modifiers, and targeted compounds were shown to either upregulate or downregulate its expression.
CONCLUSION: CK19 is a critical biomarker in a wide array of epithelial malignancies. Its differential expression correlates with tumor differentiation, metastatic behavior, and therapeutic response. These findings underscore the importance of further clinical research to validate CK19 as a diagnostic and prognostic tool, as well as a potential therapeutic target in personalized cancer management.

title: Applying the Social Ecological Model to Understand Racial Disparities Among African Americans in Lung Cancer Outcomes in the U.S: A Systematic Review of the Literature in the United States.
authors: Elkefi S, Gumbs CM, Scheinmann R et al.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: This systematic review applies the Social Ecological Model to synthesize evidence on the multiple risk factors contributing to racial disparities in lung cancer outcomes in the United States for African Americans specifically.
METHODS: We conducted a PRISMA-guided systematic review to synthesize factors associated with racial disparities in lung cancer outcomes among African Americans in the United States using the Social Ecological Model (SEM). On March 5, 2025, we searched PubMed, PsycINFO, CINAHL, Web of Science, ProQuest, and Scopus. We included U.S.-based, English-language, peer-reviewed studies that examined lung cancer disparities and contributing factors among African Americans. Two reviewers independently screened titles/abstracts and full texts (κ = 0.81 and κ = 0.86, respectively). Data were extracted using a standardized SEM-guided abstraction form, with each record reviewed by at least two extractors.
RESULTS: A final number of 82 studies (1983-2025) met the inclusion criteria. Studies documented disparities in incidence/risk, screening and diagnostic follow-up, stage at diagnosis, receipt of guideline-concordant treatment, and survival/mortality. Contributing factors clustered across SEM levels, most frequently at the individual (n = 69) and organizational (n = 40) levels, with additional community (n = 25), interpersonal (n = 23), and policy (n = 15) determinants, including community-level factors (e.g., residential segregation and neighborhood deprivation/violence), organizational barriers (e.g., access to care), and policy-level constraints (e.g., insurance coverage and screening eligibility policies).
CONCLUSIONS: Lung cancer inequities among African Americans reflect cumulative, multilevel influences. SEM-informed strategies that simultaneously address individual risk and mistrust, care delivery fragmentation, community-level deprivation, and policy barriers are needed to reduce disparities in lung cancer prevention, screening, and outcomes.

title: Less Versus More Intensive Strategies for Follow-up of Small Pulmonary Nodules : A Cluster Randomized Pragmatic Clinical Trial.
authors: Gould MK, Kelly K, Qi L et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The current less intensive guidelines for pulmonary nodule follow-up have not been compared with more intensive strategies.
OBJECTIVE: To determine whether less intensive follow-up of small pulmonary nodules is noninferior to more intensive follow-up.
DESIGN: Unblinded, cluster randomized, pragmatic comparative effectiveness trial. (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT02623712).
SETTING: 24 clusters of U.S. hospitals and health care systems.
PARTICIPANTS: 34 686 patients with a new pulmonary nodule measuring 15 mm or less, detected incidentally or by screening.
INTERVENTION: Follow-up protocols were modeled on current and prior recommendations from the Fleischner Society and the Lung CT Screening Reporting and Data System (Lung-RADS). Each cluster was randomly assigned to the less or more intensive follow-up protocol.
MEASUREMENTS: The primary outcome was the proportion of lung cancers measuring more than 20 mm at diagnosis. Analyses were conducted using mixed-effects logistic regression. The prespecified noninferiority margin was 5 percentage points.
RESULTS: A total of 34 686 participants (50.8% women) were enrolled, with a mean age of 64.5 years (SD, 11.7). Lung cancer was diagnosed within 27 months of nodule identification in 273 of 17 841 participants (1.5%) in the less intensive group and 231 of 16 845 (1.4%) in the more intensive group. Among participants with lung cancer with available data, 97 of 267 (36.3%) in the less intensive group and 62 of 224 (27.7%) in the more intensive group had cancers larger than 20 mm at diagnosis. After adjustment, more lung cancers larger than 20 mm were identified with less intensive screening (7 percentage points [95% CI, -2.0 to 15.9 percentage points]), exceeding the noninferiority margin but not statistically significant.
LIMITATIONS: Suboptimal adherence, limited power, and residual confounding.
CONCLUSION: Small, malignant pulmonary nodules frequently progress during follow-up. Although neither follow-up strategy was clearly superior, these data raise concerns about the less intensive recommendations for follow-up of small nodules.
PRIMARY FUNDING SOURCE: Patient-Centered Outcomes Research Institute.

title: Evaluating Predictors of Tumor in Patients With Anti-GABA-B Receptor Encephalitis.
authors: Zhang Y, Kong Y, Yu S et al.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Anti-GABA-B receptor encephalitis is a rare but severe autoimmune encephalitis subtype with a close association with malignancy, particularly small-cell lung cancer. This study aimed to characterize tumor-associated clinical features and identify practical warning signs for tumor occurrence in patients with anti-GABA-B receptor encephalitis.
METHODS: We retrospectively enrolled 66 consecutive patients diagnosed with anti-GABA-B receptor encephalitis between July 2013 and July 2025. Demographic characteristics, clinical manifestations, cerebrospinal fluid and serum findings, neuroimaging and electroencephalographic features, tumor-screening results, treatment, and outcomes were compared between patients with and without tumors.
RESULTS: Among 66 patients, 38 (57.6%) were diagnosed with tumors, including 36 with small-cell lung cancer. The tumor group was older (p = 0.021) and more frequently presented with sleep disorders (33/38, 86.8% vs. 18/28, 64.3%, p = 0.031), decreased consciousness (27/38, 71.1% vs. 13/28, 46.4%, p = 0.043), and hyponatremia (22/38, 57.9% vs. 9/28, 32.1%, p = 0.038). Serum paraneoplastic antibodies were more common in patients with tumors, and tumor markers including NSE (16/34, 47.1% vs 0/24, 0%, p < 0.001) and ProGRP (23/34, 67.6% vs 3/24, 12.5%, p < 0.001) were more frequently elevated. AI-assisted CT analysis provided additional support for lung cancer screening. During follow-up, patients with tumors had poorer outcomes (p < 0.001) and higher mortality (p < 0.001).
CONCLUSION: Advanced age, severe clinical presentation, elevated tumor markers, and coexisting serum paraneoplastic antibodies may help identify patients who require intensive and repeated tumor screening. AI-assisted CT diagnostic techniques may further improve early lung cancer detection, but prospective validation is required.

title: Navigating advanced lung cancer: Insights for nurses.
authors: Camp-Lelond S, Hyman J
abstract: Advanced lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer mortality in Canada, with most patients diagnosed at late stages and experiencing limited survival. Despite advances in precision oncology, fewer than 10% of patients benefit from actionable mutations, reinforcing the need for comprehensive supportive care. This paper examines a patient-centred, nursing-led approach to advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), emphasizing early integration of palliative care alongside disease-directed therapy. The illness trajectory for individuals with advanced non-small cell lung cancer is marked by worsening symptom burden, particularly dyspnea, cough, pain, and psychological distress, which significantly impairs quality of life. Oncology nurses play a pivotal role in addressing multidimensional needs related to these symptoms through early assessment, patient education, symptom management, and coordination of care. This review highlights evidence-based pharmacological and non-pharmacological interventions for key symptoms these lung cancer patients experience. Multidisciplinary and nurse-led strategies, such as breathing techniques, psychosocial support, opioid use for refractory dyspnea, and structured pain management, are essential to reducing patient distress and promoting self-management. Furthermore, effective communication and shared decision-making ensure alignment of care with patient values and realistic expectations of palliative-intent therapies. A palliative approach to nursing care in NSCLC requires proactive identification of clinical decline, structured communication, and coordinated interdisciplinary care. Ultimately, integrating early palliative care, optimizing symptom management, and strengthening nurse-led models are critical to improving outcomes, enhancing quality of life, and addressing persistent gaps in care for patients with advanced lung cancer.

title: Perioperative Patient-Reported Symptoms and Short-Term Recovery After Lung Cancer Surgery: A Longitudinal Cohort Study.
authors: Liu X, Yang Y, Wang J et al.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To determine whether perioperative patient-reported symptoms provide incremental prognostic information beyond clinical and surgical characteristics for three short-term recovery outcomes after lung cancer surgery: discharge quality of recovery, prolonged postoperative stay, and 30-day readmission.
METHODS: This retrospective single-center longitudinal cohort included 413 adults who underwent lung cancer resection in 2023. Fifteen symptoms were rated on a 0-10 numeric rating scale at seven perioperative timepoints. Outcomes were the Quality of Recovery-15 (QoR-15) score at discharge, prolonged postoperative stay (longer than 7 days), and all-cause 30-day readmission. Clinical-only models were compared with symptom-augmented models that added symptoms measured before each prediction timepoint, using L2-penalized regression and repeated five-fold nested cross-validation.
RESULTS: Discharge QoR-15 was available for 382 patients; 96 of 413 patients (23.2%) had a prolonged stay and 38 of 407 (9.3%) were readmitted. Adding postoperative day (POD) 3 symptoms increased the cross-validated R2 for discharge QoR-15 from 0.133 to 0.349; most of the increment was retained (0.171 of 0.216) when symptom domains overlapping with QoR-15 were excluded. Moderate-to-severe POD3 dyspnea, disturbed sleep, cough, and fatigue were associated with adjusted QoR-15 scores 6.8-7.8 points lower than mild symptoms; these point estimates exceeded the minimal clinically important difference. Adding POD1 symptoms increased the area under the curve (AUC) for prolonged stay from 0.679 to 0.751, and adding discharge symptoms increased the AUC for readmission from 0.616 to 0.777 in an exploratory analysis. Symptom-augmented models showed higher net benefit across clinically relevant thresholds.
LIMITATIONS: The study was retrospective and single-center, readmission events were few, and no external validation was performed.
CONCLUSION: Time-specific perioperative symptom profiles provided clinically relevant prognostic information beyond routinely available clinical and surgical characteristics. POD1, POD3, and discharge are candidate windows for symptom-informed risk updating and targeted follow-up, but prospective multicenter validation is required before clinical use.

title: Mediating Effects of Psychological Resilience in Sleep Quality and Cancer-Related Fatigue in Lung Cancer Patients: A Cross-Sectional Study.
authors: Li H, Kang H, Zhang N et al.
abstract:
PURPOSE: The purpose of this study was to examine the incidence of cancer-related fatigue (CRF) in lung cancer patients and the mediating role of psychological resilience between sleep quality and CRF.
PATIENTS AND METHODS: A convenience sampling method was used to select 272 lung cancer patients who received treatment in a hospital in Wuxi City between October 2023 and May 2024 as the study subjects. The research tools included a self-administered general information questionnaire, the Chinese-adapted Cancer Fatigue Scale (CFS), the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), and the Psychological Resilience Scale (CD-RISC). SPSS 26.0 was used to perform descriptive analysis, independent samples t-test, One-way ANOVA and correlation analysis on the collected data, and Bootstrap method was used to verify the mediating effect of psychological resilience between sleep quality and CRF.
RESULTS: The incidence of CRF in 272 patients was 93.4%, and the total CFS score was 26.87 ± 5.46. Correlation analysis showed a significant negative correlation between CRF and psychological resilience (r = -0.729, P < 0.01), and a significant positive correlation with quality of sleep (r = 0.632, P < 0.01); quality of sleep and psychological resilience showed a significant negative correlation (r = -0.722, P < 0.01). Mediation analysis showed that sleep quality indirectly affected CRF through psychological resilience, and psychological resilience had a significant mediating effect between sleep quality and CRF, accounting for 75.70% of the total effect.
CONCLUSION: More than 90% of lung cancer patients have cancer-related fatigue, and there is an association between sleep quality, psychological resilience, and cancer-related fatigue; future studies can use targeted psychological interventions oriented to sleep interventions to improve the psychological resilience of lung cancer patients and alleviate the adverse effects of cancer-related fatigue on patients.

title: An ePRO-enabled four-tier rural oncology network in China: a case report.
authors: Shen Z, Wu C, Shi J et al.
abstract: Rural oncology patients in China often encounter multiple barriers to continuous care, including fragmented healthcare delivery, geographic isolation, and limited access to specialized medical resources. Conventional hospital-centered care models may not fully address the need for continuous and coordinated management in these patients, highlighting the need for integrated healthcare approaches. The ePRO-enabled four-tier rural oncology network represents an innovative care model that combines digital symptom monitoring with hierarchical medical collaboration, involving village clinics, township health centers, county hospitals, and municipal hospitals. This article presents a case report, rather than a formal program evaluation, illustrating the application of this model in a rural patient with advanced lung cancer and demonstrating how caregiver-assisted ePRO reporting, timely clinical response, and coordinated referral supported symptom management and may have contributed to rebuilding the patient's confidence in treatment. This case provides practical insights into the potential application of ePRO-supported integrated care models for improving continuity and accessibility of oncology services in resource-limited settings.

title: "Qualitative analysis of practices in thoracic oncology regarding the discontinuation of oncological treatments and coordination with the palliative care teams".
authors: Dampierre J, Guisier F, Gambirasio MA et al.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Recent advances in first-line therapies for metastatic non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) have improved overall survival, yet response rates diminish across successive treatment lines. Oncologists are therefore often confronted with the question of discontinuing systemic therapy, a process that raises medical, relational, and ethical challenges. Despite the recognized detrimental impact of end-of-life chemotherapy on quality of life, few studies have explored physicians' practices and decision-making processes regarding treatment discontinuation and the integration of palliative care.
METHODS: We conducted a qualitative study based on semi-structured interviews with thoracic oncologists from three hospitals in Normandy, France. Interviews were recorded and transcribed verbatim. A descriptive analysis was conducted, drawing on grounded theory methodology. Data collection and analysis were performed iteratively, allowing categories and a theoretical model to emerge.
RESULTS: Due to data saturation, 10 out of 14 interviews were conducted. Analysis highlighted two meta-categories: experiences and perceptions, and responses. - Experiences and perceptions: Physicians described anticipatory communication strategies, introducing the possibility of discontinuation from earlier treatment lines. Decisions were framed using objective clinical arguments to avoid subjective projection. Physicians reported ambivalent experiences: conviction when discontinuation was clearly beneficial, but also doubt, frustration, or a sense of therapeutic failure, particularly in younger patients. Patients' reactions varied, from acceptance (often facilitated by clinical decline) to resistance or requests for second opinions. Families could act as either facilitators or barriers. The term "palliative care" was consistently associated by patients with imminent death. - Responses: Oncologists developed strategies to prevent perceived abandonment, including continued follow-up after discontinuation, transitional therapeutic breaks, or minimal treatments for symbolic continuity. The role of multidisciplinary tumor boards was considered limited, except for complex or young cases. All participants underlined the supportive role of palliative care teams in managing symptoms, maintaining continuity, and alleviating the burden on oncologists. Early integration was viewed as beneficial, though hindered by territorial disparities and resource limitations.
CONCLUSION: Discontinuation of systemic therapy in thoracic oncology is less a therapeutic withdrawal than a relationally protected transition, conceptualized as a "therapeutic transition that protects relational commitment". Early and equitable integration of palliative care appears essential to support patients, families, and oncologists during this critical phase, ensuring continuity and mitigating the risk of perceived abandonment.
