title: Localized lipid nanoparticle delivery of membrane bound IL-12 and T cell engager mRNA potentiates adoptive cell therapy in solid tumors.
authors: Metzloff AE, Berjis A, Scholler J et al.
abstract: Adoptive cell therapy (ACT), which includes T cell receptor (TCR), chimeric antigen receptor (CAR), and tumor infiltrating lymphocyte (TIL) therapy, has emerged as a promising form of immunotherapy for the treatment of cancer, with multiple FDA approvals across the three classes. However, each class faces its own specific hurdles for the treatment of solid tumors. Here, we investigated whether intratumoral administration of mRNA lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) encoding immune-stimulatory proteins would be a strategy to boost the efficacy of ACT for the treatment of solid tumors. As proof-of-concept to demonstrate the validity of this LNP strategy, we designed and validated mRNAs encoding a novel membrane-bound single-chain human IL-12 (mbIL-12) to reprogram the suppressive tumor microenvironment, as well as an anti-human mesothelin-CD3ε bispecific T cell engager (MSLN-TE) with the potential to address antigenic heterogeneity. We investigated intratumoral administration of mbIL-12 and MSLN-TE mRNA LNPs in the setting of the clinical stage NY-ESO-1 8F TCR, observing robust improvements in TCR T cell therapy efficacy upon intratumoral LNP administration in a murine xenograft model of human lung adenocarcinoma. While delivery of each mRNA construct individually improved TCR T cell therapy efficacy, combined delivery of both constructs resulted in an additive improvement in efficacy. This work sets the stage for the application of mRNA LNP technology to improve the efficacy of ACTs.

title: Antibiotic Aerosol Resets Microbial Dysregulation in Metastatic Lungs, Potentiating Anti-PD-1-Driven T Memory Stem Cell-Associated Tumor Regressions.
authors: Le Noci V, Heuser-Loy C, Bernardo G et al.
abstract:
UNLABELLED: The gut microbiota can profoundly influence the efficacy of treatment with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI), but the impact of bacteria residing within lung tumors remains largely unexplored. In this study, we show that bacteria colonizing mouse lung metastases hinder antitumor immunity by promoting regulatory T-cell (Treg) differentiation and function through metabolites, including valine. Antibiotic inhalation, a strategy to achieve high airway concentration with limited effects on the gut microbiota, reduced Treg frequencies, expanded stem-like T cells, broadened the T-cell receptor repertoire, and boosted complete remission rates following programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) blockade. Replacing tumor-associated bacteria, transplanting Tregs, or depleting T cells dampened the efficacy of the anti-PD-1/antibiotics combination, whereas the adoptive transfer of T cells from combination-treated mice into naïve mice conferred protection against tumor challenge. DNA sequences consistent with tumor-associated bacteria in mouse metastases were detected in 33 of 95 human lung cancer specimens, which exhibited increased Treg and reduced T-cell infiltration. Our findings reveal that tumor-associated microbes represent a barrier to ICI therapy that can be removed by disrupting intratumoral bacterial dysregulation with aerosolized antibiotics.
SIGNIFICANCE: Tumor-associated bacteria promote intratumoral Treg accumulation, limiting PD-1 blockade efficacy, and inhaled antibiotics break this immunosuppressive axis, thereby boosting T-cell control of lung metastasis upon checkpoint blockade.

title: Marked worsening of depression in a patient with lung cancer following discontinuation of olanzapine as an antiemetic: a case report and mini literature review.
authors: Yamaguchi J, Sadahiro R, Matsuoka H
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Nausea is a common physical symptom that develops during cancer treatment. Olanzapine, an antipsychotic drug, is often prescribed as an antiemetic to treat nausea during cancer treatment. However, patients with cancer are prone to emotional instability, and in some cases, olanzapine may inadvertently contribute to the improvement of psychiatric symptoms.
CASE DESCRIPTION: The present case included a woman in her 40s with no history of psychiatric disorders. At X-3 years, she was diagnosed with lung cancer following an abnormal finding during a health screening. After undergoing a left upper lobe lobectomy, she was treated with carboplatin + pemetrexed sodium hemipentahydrate + bevacizumab. At X-1 years, she developed nausea as a side effect of chemotherapy, and olanzapine (2.5 mg/day, orally) was initiated. Although the patient was aware of depressive mood, insomnia, and anxiety around the onset of nausea, the symptoms were not fully disclosed to healthcare providers. At her request, olanzapine was continued even after the completion of chemotherapy, and she experienced improvement of the psychiatric symptoms following the initiation of olanzapine. At X years, multiple lung metastases were detected, and anticancer drug therapy was discontinued. Olanzapine was also discontinued because the nausea was no longer present. Subsequently, the patient gradually developed depression, insomnia, anxiety, and intense restlessness. The psychiatric symptoms improved following the resumption of olanzapine in combination with antidepressants and anxiolytics.
CONCLUSIONS: Olanzapine, prescribed for nausea, may unintentionally be effective in the improvement of psychiatric symptoms. When discontinuing olanzapine administered as an antiemetic to patients with cancer, oncologists need to ensure that the psychiatric symptoms do not worsen.

title: CAR-based cellular therapy against breast cancer: a translational roadmap for engineering and clinical development.
authors: Martin-Quesada AI, Mulvey A, Martinez-Useros J et al.
abstract: CAR-T cell therapy has transformed clinical outcomes in selected hematologic malignancies, but its translation to breast cancer remains limited by antigen heterogeneity, on-target/off-tumor toxicity, poor tumor trafficking, and an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. In this review, we provide a translational roadmap for CAR-based therapy in breast cancer, spanning target selection, therapeutic engineering, and clinical development. We performed a narrative targeted review of preclinical breast cancer models, clinical trials, conference abstracts, and registered CAR-based cellular therapy studies relevant to breast cancer, with evidence updated through 30 June 2026. The evidence was synthesized according to antigen selection, antigen density and safety, route of administration, engineering strategies, and biomarker-driven trial design. Preclinical models support the feasibility of CAR-based approaches in antigen-enriched settings, with activity reported against HER2, MUC1/MUC1*, ROR1, EGFR, c-MET, TROP2, B7-H3, Nectin-4, GD2, and mesothelin. Early clinical studies demonstrate that the administration is feasible with monitoring; however, objective responses remain uncommon, disease stabilization is the most frequent outcome, and clinically significant toxicities have occurred in selected programs. The most plausible near-term opportunities include HER2-positive disease with CNS or leptomeningeal involvement, antigen-enriched triple-negative breast cancer, and selected locoregional or high-antigen-density settings. Next-generation affinity-tuned, logic-gated, switchable, armored, and gene-edited platforms are being developed to improve tumor selectivity, trafficking, persistence, and resistance to immunosuppression. Overall, CAR-based therapy for breast cancer remains investigational, and future clinical trials should prospectively integrate quantitative target assessment, disease site, relevant biological and clinical barriers, manufacturing feasibility, and route of delivery to guide CAR-platform selection and correlative evaluation.

title: Expanded NK and fratricide-resistant CD70 CAR-NK cells are potent against patient-derived glioblastoma cells in vitro and in vivo.
authors: Mehboob M, Rätsep M, Moinuddin A et al.
abstract: Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) is a highly aggressive brain tumor characterized by pervasive tumor recurrence and very poor patient survival. While αβ T cell-based chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) immunotherapies show efficacy in hematologic malignancies, manufacturing delays and potential fatal immune overactivation have prompted the exploration of alternative cell sources, including natural killer (NK) cells. NK cells represent an emerging cell source due to their potent antigen-independent intrinsic cytotoxicity, self-regulating inhibitory mechanisms, and low risk of graft-versus-host disease. In this study, we expanded peripheral blood NK cells using K562 feeder cells expressing membrane-bound IL-21 (K562-mb-IL-21) to produce highly activated and metabolically robust cells targeting both cell lines and patient-derived GBM tumor cells. Furthermore, our in vitro results demonstrate the broad targeting potential of our expanded NK cells, as they exhibit cytotoxicity against a cell line and patient-derived sample of another aggressive brain tumor, medulloblastoma (MB). To enhance tumor-directed cytotoxicity, we utilized CRISPR/Cas9 and adeno-associated virus-based gene delivery to generate stable anti-CD70 CAR-NK cells. CD70 is a promising target due to its minimal expression in healthy tissues and overexpression in recurrent GBM. However, NK cells gain CD70 surface expression upon expansion, causing anti-CD70 CAR-NK cell fratricide. Subsequently, knocking out the CD70 gene enabled large-scale expansion of anti-CD70 CAR-NK cells that were functional against both in vitro and in vivo GBM models.

title: Locoregional administration of bispecific CAR-T cells targeting CD44 and CD133 in recurrent high-grade glioma: a first-in-human investigator-initiated trial.
authors: Zhai Y, Li G, Wang A et al.
abstract: Grade IV glioma remains highly lethal, and effective therapies for recurrent disease remain limited. Glioma stem cells (GSCs) contribute to therapeutic resistance and tumor recurrence, providing a rationale for GSC-targeted immunotherapy. We conducted a single-center, single-arm investigator-initiated trial evaluating locoregional administration of CD44/CD133 bispecific chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells incorporating a truncated interleukin-7 receptor α (IL-7Rα) intracellular domain in ten adults with recurrent grade IV glioma. Treatment was well tolerated, with no dose-limiting toxicities or Grade ≥2 cytokine release syndrome. Adverse events were predominantly mild and transient, and no patient required IL-6 or IL-1 blockade. CAR-T cell leakage into peripheral blood remained minimal, whereas cerebrospinal fluid cytokine elevations were modest following infusion. Three patients achieved partial responses. The median overall survival after the first CAR-T cell infusion was 465 days. Exploratory single-cell RNA sequencing and proteomic analyses suggested patient stratification in macrophage-associated signatures, particularly in interferon signaling and antigen-presentation programs, which were associated with distinct clinical outcomes independently of IDH mutation status in this cohort. These findings demonstrate the feasibility and safety of repeated locoregional administration of GSC-targeting IL-7Rα-armored bispecific CAR-T cells. Exploratory immune profiling further identified inter-patient heterogeneity in macrophage-associated immune programs, which warrants validation in larger prospective studies. (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT05577091, NMPA No. CXSL2500032).

title: Rewiring resistance in solid tumors: CAR-NK strategies for immune evasion and tumor microenvironmental barriers.
authors: Kokkanti RR, Biswas S, Parida N et al.
abstract: Clinical translation of adoptive cellular immunotherapy in solid tumors remains constrained by a hierarchical resistance architecture comprising antigen heterogeneity, extracellular matrix (ECM) mediated transport barriers, immune suppression, and spatial exclusion. Although chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapies have demonstrated durable clinical responses in hematological malignancies, their efficacy in solid tumors remains limited by impaired cellular trafficking, restricted tissue penetration, heterogeneous intratumoral distribution, and profound microenvironmental suppression. Natural killer (NK) cells complement CAR-T therapy through major histocompatibility complex (MHC) independent tumor recognition, improved targeting of antigen-low tumor cells, and dynamic interactions with the tumor microenvironment. Building on these complementary properties, we introduce a Resistance-Solution Mapping Framework (RSMF) that systematically links major resistance barriers with engineering strategies designed to overcome them, while reframing engineered CAR-NK cells as programmable, living drug delivery systems. Unlike conventional reviews that catalogue engineering technologies, this framework evaluates how multi-antigen targeting, cytokine armoring, chemokine receptor engineering, and related approaches can modulate cellular pharmacokinetics, including tumor-directed trafficking, target-site accumulation and functional persistence within complex solid tumor ecosystems. We further critically assess the predictive value and translational limitations of advanced preclinical platforms, including patient-derived organoids and xenograft models, for evaluating immune-cell trafficking, matrix penetration, metabolic fitness, and therapeutic durability. Collectively, this review provides a systems-level roadmap integrating cellular engineering, tumor transport biology, and drug delivery principles to guide the rational development of next-generation CAR-NK therapies for overcoming multifactorial resistance in solid tumors.

title: Baseline PD-L1 expression and survival outcomes in ALK-rearranged, advanced non-small cell lung cancer treated with first-line ALK tyrosine kinase inhibitors: A nationwide cohort study.
authors: Zhang T, Qiu Y, Lin T et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The prognostic value of programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) expression in anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK)-rearranged, advanced non-small cell lung cancer (aNSCLC) treated with first-line ALK tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) remains unclear, and existing observational studies have methodological limitations.
METHODS: The authors conducted a nationwide cohort study using deidentified electronic health record-derived data from the US Flatiron Health database covering August 2011 through March 2025. Eligible patients had stage III-IV ALK-rearranged aNSCLC, initiated first-line ALK-TKI therapy, and had pretreatment PD-L1 results. Patients were classified into a low (tumor proportion score, <50%) or high (tumor proportion score, ≥50%) PD-L1 expression group. Inverse probability weighting (IPW) was used to balance measured confounders between groups. Weighted Kaplan-Meier analyses and Cox proportional hazards models were used to evaluate real-world progression-free survival and overall survival.
RESULTS: Among 106,901 patients, 2117 had ALK rearrangements. Of these, 552 who had baseline PD-L1 results were included, with 344 (62.3%) in the low PD-L1 group and 208 (37.7%) in the high PD-L1 group. High PD-L1 expression was associated with poorer overall survival (median, 36.3 vs. 56.1 months; IPW-adjusted hazard ratio for low vs. high expression, 0.71; 95% confidence interval, 0.54-0.95; p = .021). The difference in real-world progression-free survival was not significant (low vs. high expression, 17.1 vs. 22.9 months, respectively; IPW-adjusted hazard ratio for low vs. high expression, 0.91; 95% confidence interval, 0.71-1.15; p = .431). The results were generally consistent across subgroup and sensitivity analyses.
CONCLUSIONS: High baseline PD-L1 expression was associated with poorer overall survival in patients with ALK-rearranged aNSCLC who were receiving first-line ALK-TKI therapy.

title: Revealing HOXC6 Overexpression and Its Downstream Targets in Small Cell Lung Cancer Through Single-Cell Sequencing-Based Virtual Knockout and CRISPR-Cas9 Analysis.
authors: Wu KJ, Huang WY, Chen YY et al.
abstract: Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) is a highly aggressive malignancy characterized by frequent recurrence and rapid development of therapeutic resistance, underscoring an urgent need to identify stable and reliable molecular biomarkers and actionable therapeutic targets. Homeobox C6 (HOXC6), an important transcription factor of the Homeobox (HOX) family, has not yet been systematically investigated with respect to its expression pattern and biological functions in SCLC. To systematically evaluate differential HOXC6 expression in SCLC; to delineate its cellular origin and functional characteristics at the single-cell level. RNA-seq and microarray data from multiple platforms were integrated to comprehensively analyze HOXC6 mRNA expression, followed by immunohistochemical validation using SCLC and non-SCLC tissue samples from our institution. Quantitative real-time PCR and Transwell migration assays were performed to validate HOXC6 expression and evaluate its effect on the migratory capacity of NCI-H446 cells. SCLC single-cell RNA-sequencing data were analyzed to identify the cellular source of HOXC6, and functional enrichment analyses were performed on genes positively correlated with HOXC6 expression. In silico knockout of HOXC6 was conducted at the single-cell level using scTenifoldKnk, and the predicted transcriptomic alterations were evaluated through differential expression and gene set enrichment analyses. CellChat and scMetabolism were applied to characterize cell-cell communication networks and metabolic pathway activities, respectively. Immune and stromal infiltration patterns were systematically assessed using CIBERSORT, MCP-counter, xCell, EPIC, quanTIseq, and ESTIMATE, while immune evasion-related phenotypes were evaluated using TIDE. Finally, ChIP-seq data were integrated with CRISPR dependency screening results for multi-omics cross-validation. Protein-protein molecular docking was subsequently performed to explore potential structural associations of HOXC6 with ACP5 and ZEB2, followed by a 100-ns molecular dynamics simulation of the HOXC6-ACP5 complex to evaluate its predicted conformational stability. Bulk transcriptomic analysis showed that HOXC6 expression was higher in 202 SCLC tissues than in 127 non-SCLC tissues. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated predominantly nuclear localization of HOXC6 in tumor cells and elevated HOXC6 expression in SCLC. Single-cell analysis revealed that HOXC6 was mainly enriched in neuroendocrine-like cell populations, whereas functional enrichment of HOXC6-positively correlated genes highlighted axonogenesis, microtubule and cytoskeletal organization, and establishment of cell polarity. Following the in silico single-cell knockout of HOXC6, specific transcriptional alterations were computationally predicted, accompanied by enrichment of T-cell proliferation-related pathways. Multi-algorithm immune infiltration analysis further showed that elevated HOXC6 expression was associated with reduced overall immune and stromal signals and cell type-specific remodeling of the tumor microenvironment, although no significant association with the overall TIDE score was observed. In cell-cell communication analyses, the HOXC6-high neuroendocrine-like cell population exhibited hub-like interaction patterns, with the macrophage migration inhibitory factor signaling axis identified as a major communication pathway. Metabolic pathway scoring further indicated that HOXC6 expression was associated with differential activation of glycolysis/gluconeogenesis and oxidative phosphorylation. Integration of ChIP-seq profiles, expression correlations, and CRISPR dependency screening revealed that ACP5 and ZEB2 were generally expressed at low levels in SCLC and were both upregulated following HOXC6 knockout. Enriched HOXC6-binding signals were detected at the ACP5 and ZEB2 loci, and HOXC6 expression was generally negatively correlated with both genes across multiple independent datasets. CRISPR dependency screening additionally indicated that higher ACP5 expression was associated with a suppressive phenotype in SCLC-related cells. Molecular docking predicted a potential interaction between HOXC6 and ACP5, while the subsequent 100-ns molecular dynamics simulation indicated that the HOXC6-ACP5 complex maintained a relatively stable binding conformation over the simulation period. HOXC6 is overexpressed in SCLC and may contribute to the migratory phenotype of SCLC cells. It may also participate in neuroendocrine-associated transcriptional programs, immunosuppressive features, intercellular communication, and metabolic reprogramming. The integrated regulatory, dependency, molecular-docking, and molecular-dynamics evidence further prioritizes ACP5 as a candidate HOXC6-associated molecule, although the predicted interaction requires direct experimental validation.

title: A Study of ZW209 in Participants With Advanced Solid Tumors
summary: The purpose of this study is to find out if ZW209, an antibody designed to direct patient T cells to target and destroy DLL3 expressing cancer cells is safe and can treat participants with advanced cancers, including small cell lung cancer.

title: Spatial heterogeneity and prognostic value of tertiary lymphoid structures in peritumoral inflammation and tumor beds after neoadjuvant immunochemotherapy for resectable NSCLC.
authors: Xie M, Gao J, Zhang Y et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Tertiary lymphoid structures (TLS) are associated with favorable outcomes in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) following neoadjuvant immunochemotherapy. However, the biological and prognostic differences between TLS in peritumoral inflammation (PI) and the tumor bed (TB) remain unclear.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: We analyzed 254 patients with NSCLC from three centers: 98 treated with neoadjuvant immunochemotherapy (NICT), 54 treated with neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NCT), and 102 treatment-naïve patients. PI and TB TLS abundance and maturation were assessed in relation to pathological response and survival. Exploratory spatial transcriptomics characterized their cellular composition and intercellular communication.
RESULTS: PI was more prevalent in the NICT cohort (77.5%) than in the NCT (50.0%) and treatment-naïve (26.5%) cohorts (p < 0.001). In the NICT cohort, PI TLS were more abundant and mature than TB TLS. Multivariable analysis showed that PI-related TLS were independently associated with recurrence-free survival (RFS) after adjustment for major pathological response, TB TLS abundance, and other clinicopathological factors. A nomogram incorporating ypN stage and PI-related features achieved areas under the curve (AUCs) of 0.894, 0.884, and 0.887 for predicting 1-, 2-, and 3-year RFS, respectively. Spatial transcriptomics revealed distinct transcriptional and immune profiles, with PI TLS showing greater plasma cell abundance and more active interactions with the tumor microenvironment than TB TLS.
CONCLUSION: In resectable NSCLC, NICT was associated with a higher prevalence of PI and greater TLS abundance and maturation. PI TLS showed greater prognostic value and a more immune-active microenvironment than TB TLS, supporting spatial TLS assessment for postoperative risk stratification.

title: [The EU-funded CONNECT study: Digital monitoring of immune-related adverse events during immunotherapy for stage IV non-small cell lung cancer and advanced pleural mesothelioma].
authors: Wesseler C, Reinmuth N, Geßler N et al.
abstract: For both advanced stage IV non-small lung cancer (NSCLC) and advanced, inoperable pleural mesothelioma, (chemo-)immunotherapy has recently become standard of care and has significantly improved the prognosis. However, in the course of treatment, disease progression and/or immune-related adverse events (irAEs) often occur, which ultimately influence the prognosis and the course of treatment. As many patients and their primary health care providers are unfamiliar with the specific symptoms, oncology medical staff regularly only become aware of them on the occasion of scheduled routine examinations. This issue is addressed by the EU-funded, two-center CONNECT study, which started in July 2026 and is currently open for recruitment. It investigates the effectiveness and feasibility of a symptom-oriented, app- and smartwatch-based digital monitoring during treatment.

title: Tumor cell membrane-coated dual-adjuvant nanovaccine for lung cancer immunotherapy.
authors: Fu J, Zhu S, Cheng W et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide, highlighting the urgent need for more potent immunotherapeutic strategies to overcome the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment.
METHODS: In this study, we developed a biomimetic dual-adjuvant nanovaccine (VPL7AM) based on a polymeric core coated with murine lung cancer cell membranes. The core was constructed using a STING agonist heterocyclic derivative (7 A) conjugated polymer, electrostatically complexed with monophosphoryl lipid A (MPLA), a TLR4 agonist. The tumor cell membrane provided a full spectrum of tumor-associated antigens while effectively masking the intrinsic cationic charge of the polymeric carrier.
RESULTS: Physicochemical characterization confirmed the successful synthesis of the PL7A polymer and the formation of a stable core-shell nanostructure with an average size of approximately 100 nm. Membrane coating significantly reversed the surface charge from positive (+9 mV) to negative (-7 mV), thereby reducing the inherent cytotoxicity and hemolytic activity associated with the polylysine backbone. In vitro studies demonstrated excellent biocompatibility and reduced nonspecific membrane disruption. Importantly, the nanovaccine synergistically activated STING and TLR4 signaling pathways, leading to enhanced dendritic cell maturation and increased secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines.
CONCLUSION: This biomimetic platform provides a safe and efficient delivery system for dual adjuvants and personalized tumor antigens. It represents a promising dual-activation strategy for synergistic immunotherapy against lung cancer.

title: Divergence between historical disease burden and future prevention opportunities in COPD and lung cancer.
authors: Xie Y, Huang P, Tan J et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and tracheal, bronchus, and lung cancer (TBL) share modifiable risk factors, yet countries differ in historical disease burden and prevention gains.
OBJECTIVE: We aimed to distinguish historical respiratory burden from future prevention opportunities.
METHODS: Using Global Burden of Disease Study 2021 (GBD 2021) estimates, we analyzed COPD-TBL burden attributable to smoking, secondhand smoke, ambient fine particulate matter (PM2.5), and household air pollution in 204 countries and territories from 1990-2021. Historical burden was derived from COPD prevalence trajectories. Prevention gaps compared projected 2030 burden under national trends with a faster Sociodemographic Index (SDI)-matched peer benchmark. Mortality and welfare differences were estimated for 2022-2030; World Health Organization (WHO) and China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS) data provided triangulation.
RESULTS: Historical validation favored the peer benchmark (log-scale mean absolute error 0.178 vs 0.220). Historical burden and prevention gap were weakly correlated after adjustment for SDI and current COPD prevalence (partial Pearson r = -0.253, 95% confidence interval (CI) -0.385 to -0.113); 128 of 204 settings (62.7%) were discordant. Higher-historical-burden groups accounted for 79.9% of 2021 welfare losses from the leading risk, whereas higher-prevention-gap groups accounted for 97.4% of attainable 2022-2030 welfare gains. The trajectory difference was 0.98 million deaths, corresponding to US$597.6 billion. In CHARLS, greater chronic lung disease history was associated with subsequent hospitalization beyond current disease status (odds ratio 1.313, 95% CI 1.100-1.566).
CONCLUSIONS: Historical burden and prevention potential were misaligned in nearly two-thirds of settings. Both dimensions can guide respiratory health planning.

title: Three-Dimensional COF/rGO/AuNP Porous Membranes for Enrichment-Enhanced Surface Enhanced Raman Scattering Detection of Aldehydes in Exhaled Breath.
authors: Deng T, Li M, Shang Y et al.
abstract: Lung cancer remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality, highlighting the need for noninvasive approaches for early disease screening. Volatile aldehydes in exhaled breath have emerged as promising biomarkers because their concentrations may reflect disease-associated metabolic changes; however, their low abundance and inefficient interaction with SERS substrates remain challenging for reliable breath analysis. Herein, a three-dimensional porous membrane composed of covalent organic framework/reduced graphene oxide/gold nanoparticles (COF/rGO/AuNP) was developed as a SERS substrate for sensitive detection of volatile aldehydes in exhaled breath. The membrane was functionalized with 4-aminothiophenol (4-ATP) for selective aldehyde capture through Schiff-base formation. The combination of COF-mediated gas enrichment and electromagnetic enhancement from AuNPs enabled ultrasensitive aldehyde detection, with a detection limit of 0.28 ppb for benzaldehyde. The platform exhibited excellent selectivity, signal uniformity, reproducibility, and resistance to humidity interference. Its practical applicability was demonstrated by analyzing exhaled breath samples from healthy volunteers and patients with lung cancer, revealing distinct differences in aldehyde concentration profiles between the two groups. This work provides a simple and sensitive membrane-based SERS platform for trace gaseous aldehyde analysis and demonstrates its potential for noninvasive breath-based lung cancer screening.

title: Pulmonary Function Estimation from Opportunistic Chest CT Using a Hybrid Image-plus-Quantitative-Feature Deep Learning Model.
authors: Carvalho ARS, Guimarães AR, Kee SL et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Spirometry is underused and most airflow obstruction remains undiagnosed. Chest CT acquired for lung cancer screening contains anatomical and densitometric information that may proxy lung function.
RESEARCH QUESTION: Can a deep learning model combining volumetric CT with CT-derived quantitative features estimate spirometric parameters and detect abnormal spirometry in independent external cohorts without retraining?
STUDY DESIGN AND METHODS: A three-dimensional convolutional neural network trained on 10,371 low-dose CT reconstructions from 5,975 National Lung Screening Trial (NLST) participants was fused with 20 lung densitometry and tracheal geometry features to predict FEV1, FVC and FEV1/FVC. The frozen model was applied to an External Lung Cancer Screening Cohort (ELCSC, n = 268) and COPDGene (n = 10,302 scans). Ablation, two spirometric-pattern subgroups and prevalence-conditional predictive values were also evaluated. Reference spirometry was pre-bronchodilator in NLST and post-bronchodilator in COPDGene. Abnormal spirometry (FEV1/FVC < 0.70, FEV1 < 80% or FVC < 80% predicted) was assessed with sensitivity, specificity and AUROC, and agreement with the concordance correlation coefficient (CCC).
RESULTS: The model detected abnormal spirometry with AUROC 0.898 (sensitivity 89.9%, specificity 66.1%) in the ELCSC and AUROC 0.913 (sensitivity 66.9%, specificity 96.3%) in COPDGene, with CCCs of 0.80-0.88 for FEV1, FVC and FEV1/FVC. In held-out development data, CCCs were 0.86/0.85/0.71 (full model) versus 0.83/0.82/0.50 image-only and 0.55/0.65/0.35 feature-only. Agreement was lower, with systematic overestimation, in a COPD subgroup (FEV1/FVC < 0.70; CCC 0.62) and in a low-FVC, preserved-ratio pattern (CCC 0.70-0.78).
INTERPRETATION: The model estimates spirometric parameters and detects abnormal spirometry across independent cohorts without retraining, with different sensitivity-specificity profiles at the same decision rule. It shows promise for opportunistic assessment of existing CT scans, but referral performance varies by population and prospective utility is unproven.
CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: COPDGene, ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT00608764.

title: Granzyme B as a predictive biomarker for therapeutic outcomes in non-small cell lung cancer patients undergoing anti-PD-1 therapy.
authors: Jain K, Singh A, Aggarwal S et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) targeting the PD-1/PD-L1 axis have transformed the management of advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). However, durable clinical benefit is restricted to a subset of patients, necessitating reliable, minimally invasive pharmacodynamic biomarkers to monitor treatment engagement and response.
METHODS: In this prospective observational study evaluating an expanded patient cohort overlapping with our previous reporting, 64 patients with advanced NSCLC receiving second-line nivolumab monotherapy and 30 healthy controls were analyzed. Peripheral blood samples were collected longitudinally at baseline (T0), 6-8 weeks (T1), and 14-16 weeks (T2) post-treatment initiation. Plasma Granzyme B (GrmB) concentrations (pg/mL) were quantified via ELISA, and cell subset-specific intracellular expression was characterized using multiparametric flow cytometry. Archival tumor tissue was evaluated for PD-L1 expression, tumor mutational burden, microsatellite instability, and TP53 status. Exploratory in-vitro experiments evaluated A549 and NCI-H23 cell lines exposed to direct nivolumab treatment (0-200 µg/mL). Longitudinal dynamics were evaluated using repeated-measures linear mixed-effects models with multiplicity adjustments, and survival outcomes (OS and PFS) were assessed using Kaplan-Meier.
RESULTS: Responders (R) demonstrated significantly higher baseline tumor PD-L1 expression compared to non-responders (NR). Flow cytometric immunophenotyping revealed dynamic expansions in responders, including a three-fold increase in CD3+CD56+ NKT-like cells, a two-fold increase in NK cells, a ten-fold elevation in CD8+Granzyme B+ T cells, and a 2.5-fold increase in proliferating Ki67+CD8+PD-1+ T cells. Circulating plasma Granzyme B concentrations were markedly elevated in responders compared to non-responders and healthy controls (P < 0.0001). In exploratory cell-line assays, direct nivolumab exposure increased Granzyme B secretion and expression in A549 and NCI-H23 cells without impacting short-term cell viability. While higher circulating Granzyme B trajectory correlated with superior progression-free and overall survival, multivariable Cox regression indicated that Granzyme B kinetics serve as a dynamic marker of active immune engagement rather than an independent pre-treatment predictive biomarker when adjusting for overall clinical response.
CONCLUSION: Longitudinal monitoring of plasma Granzyme B kinetics and cytotoxic lymphocyte activation particularly CD3+CD56+ NKT-like and effector CD+ T-cell subsets provides a valuable non-invasive pharmacodynamic indicator of systemic anti-tumor immune activation during nivolumab therapy in advanced NSCLC.

title: A syringe-based nanoliquid biopsy platform integrating magnetic immunocapture and electrochemical assay for circulating tumor cells enumeration and molecular profiling in NSCLC patients.
authors: Li C, Liu Y, Li M et al.
abstract: The number and phenotypic profile of circulating tumor cells (CTCs) have demonstrated their capability in cancer diagnosis and therapeutic efficacy assessment, while programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) and major histocompatibility complex class Ⅱ (MHC-Ⅱ) emerge as core predictive biomarkers for cancer immunotherapy response. Despite their clinical significance, simplified methodologies with potential for point-of-care (POC) adaptation that enable simultaneous detection of CTCs and these two immune-related surface proteins in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remain scarce, which was quite critical for comprehensive liquid biopsy - based cancer management. In this work, an integrated bioassay for synchronous enumeration of CTCs and quantitative profiling of PD-L1/MHC-Ⅱ expression on captured CTCs from NSCLC patient blood samples was developed. A magnetic immunocapture probe with nanorod architecture was functionalized with dual targeting aptamers, which enabled an enhanced capture efficiency toward CTCs up to 95%. Meanwhile, for differential detection of PD-L1 and MHC-Ⅱ, CdTe and PbS quantum dots (QDs) were conjugated with specific antibodies against PD-L1 and MHC-Ⅱ, respectively, with quantification enabled by electrochemical voltammetric analysis of Cd2+ and Pb2+ released from QDs. To simplify assay operation, a disposable syringe filter equipped with nitrocellulose (NC) membrane was employed as the platform for immobilizing antibodies and immuno-recognition. The robustness and efficiency of the integrated system were validated by investigating the correlations between CTC counts, PD-L1/MHC-Ⅱ expression levels, and disease progression in NSCLC patients, which highlighted its potential as a powerful tool for precision immunotherapy guidance.

title: Structured and Adapted Exercise Prehabilitation Before Pulmonary Resection in Patients With Multiple Comorbidities
summary:
The goal of this single-centre, retrospective-prospective observational case-control study is to assess changes in cardiorespiratory fitness following supervised exercise-based prehabilitation and to compare postoperative clinical outcomes in adults aged 18-85 years with multiple comorbidities (Charlson Comorbidity Index \[CCI\]\>5) who are scheduled for major pulmonary resection for suspected primary or secondary pulmonary malignancy.

The main questions it aims to answer are:

* How does maximal oxygen uptake (VO₂max), measured by cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET), change between baseline (T0) and completion of prehabilitation (T1)?
* Do the incidence of postoperative complications, postoperative length of stay, duration of pleural air leakage, pleural fluid drainage volume and chest-drain duration differ between patients receiving prehabilitation and those receiving standard perioperative care? Researchers will compare patients receiving care through an Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) pathway that includes supervised exercise-based prehabilitation with patients receiving standard perioperative care without prehabilitation. Matching analyses will be used to account for differences in recorded patient characteristics.

Participants will:

* Undergo preoperative clinical assessment. Patients assessed for prehabilitation will also undergo functional assessments, as clinically appropriate, including CPET, the treadmill six-minute walk test (T-6MWT), spirometry, bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA), handgrip dynamometry and questionnaires.

title: Association of baseline serum S100A9 levels with idiopathic acute exacerbation of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and chemotherapy-triggered acute exacerbation of interstitial lung disease.
authors: Hirakawa T, Yamaguchi K, Miura S et al.
abstract: BackgroundIdiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is a representative form of interstitial lung disease (ILD). Acute exacerbation of IPF (AE-IPF), categorized as idiopathic or triggered, can be fatal, similar to acute exacerbations observed in other forms of ILD. S100A9, a damage-associated molecular pattern, has been associated with poor prognosis in IPF and higher mortality in patients with AE-IPF. However, its association with the development of AE, particularly in idiopathic or triggered cases, remains unclear.ObjectivesThis study evaluated the association between baseline serum S100A9 levels and the development of idiopathic AE-IPF and chemotherapy-triggered AE-ILD.DesignThis was a single-center retrospective study of two independent cohorts: an IPF cohort and a cohort of ILD concomitant with lung cancer.MethodsWe analyzed 89 patients diagnosed with IPF between June 2005 and December 2020 and 52 patients with ILD concomitant with lung cancer who received cytotoxic chemotherapy between July 2010 and December 2021 at Hiroshima University Hospital. Baseline serum S100A9 levels were quantified using an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay.ResultsIdiopathic AE-IPF occurred in 10.1% of patients within two years, and chemotherapy-triggered AE-ILD occurred in 26.9% within one year. ROC analysis identified baseline serum S100A9 cut-off values of 16.7 ng/mL for idiopathic AE-IPF (AUC 0.65; sensitivity 55.6%; specificity 81.3%) and 15.2 ng/mL for chemotherapy-triggered AE-ILD (AUC 0.69; sensitivity 92.9%; specificity 47.4%). Patients with high baseline serum S100A9 levels had significantly higher incidences of idiopathic AE-IPF and chemotherapy-triggered AE-ILD than those with low levels (25.0% vs. 5.8%, p = 0.012; 39.4% vs. 5.3%, p = 0.008, respectively). In exploratory multivariable Fine-Gray regression analyses with death as a competing event, high baseline serum S100A9 levels were significantly associated with the development of idiopathic AE-IPF and chemotherapy-triggered AE-ILD.ConclusionHigh baseline serum S100A9 levels may be associated with an increased risk of idiopathic AE-IPF and chemotherapy-triggered AE-ILD.

title: Preclinical and First-in-Human Phase I Evaluation of HH-101, an Fc-Afucosylated Anti-TIGIT Monoclonal Antibody with Enhanced Effector Function.
authors: Xue R, Zhang Y, Dang Q et al.
abstract:
PURPOSE: HH-101 is an Fc-afucosylated human IgG1 monoclonal antibody targeting TIGIT with enhanced Fc-mediated effector function. We report its preclinical characterization and first-in-human phase I evaluation.
PATIENTS AND METHODS: HH-101 was evaluated in syngeneic tumor models and in nonclinical toxicology studies. In a first-in-human phase I dose-escalation study (NCT07554196), 12 patients with heavily pretreated advanced solid tumors received intravenous HH-101 every 3 weeks across four dose cohorts (0.3-10 mg/kg).
RESULTS: Afucosylated HH-101 produced greater tumor growth inhibition than Fc-wild-type or Fc-silent variants and was associated with selective depletion of intratumoral TIGIT⁺ Tregs. Clinically, treatment-related adverse events occurred in 11/12 patients (91.7%), predominantly grade 1-2; grade ≥3 events occurred in four (33.3%). One dose-limiting toxicity (grade 4 thrombocytopenia) occurred at 10 mg/kg; the maximum tolerated dose was not reached. Pharmacokinetics were dose-proportional, with a steady-state half-life of 18.0 days. Pharmacodynamic analyses showed >99% peripheral receptor occupancy and a 65%-90% reduction in circulating TIGIT⁺ Tregs. Among nine efficacy-evaluable patients, objective response rate was 0% and disease control rate was 11.1%, including stable disease lasting five cycles in a patient with thymic carcinoma.
CONCLUSIONS: HH-101 showed a manageable safety profile, dose-proportional pharmacokinetics, and target engagement accompanied by TIGIT⁺ Treg depletion, but limited single-agent activity. The recommended dose was 10 mg/kg, supporting further investigation, particularly in combination strategies.

title: Robot-assisted versus video-assisted thoracoscopic thymectomy for early-stage thymic epithelial tumours: multicentre randomized clinical trial.
authors: Wang S, Zhu J, Yue W et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: High-level evidence comparing robot-assisted (RATT) and video-assisted thoracoscopic thymectomy (VATT) for early-stage thymic epithelial tumours remains limited. This multicentre randomized clinical trial aimed to determine whether robotic assistance confers measurable biological and clinical benefits over VATT.
METHODS: In this single-blinded, parallel-group trial, adults with radiologically suspected stage I-II thymic epithelial tumours across three academic centres were randomly assigned (1 : 1) to undergo RATT or VATT. Due to the surgical nature of the interventions, participants and surgeons were unblinded. The primary outcome was total postoperative thoracic drainage volume. Key secondary outcomes included operative and recovery metrics, inflammatory markers, patient-reported quality of life, and 30-day morbidity.
RESULTS: Among 122 patients randomized (61 to RATT, 61 to VATT), all 122 were included in the intention-to-treat analysis. For the primary outcome, median postoperative drainage was significantly lower following RATT versus VATT (170 versus 266 ml, median difference -100 ml, 95% confidence interval -150 to -50; P < 0.001). For secondary outcomes, RATT significantly attenuated the systemic inflammatory response, with lower median interleukin-6 (18.7 versus 27.0 pg/ml; P = 0.045) and C-reactive protein (10.8 versus 22.4 mg/l; P = 0.002). Furthermore, RATT yielded more lymph nodes (P = 0.045), despite a longer operative time (70 versus 57 minutes; P = 0.002). Regarding harms, postoperative complication rates were similar between the RATT and VATT groups (10% versus 8%; P > 0.999).
CONCLUSION: RATT significantly reduces tissue trauma-evidenced by decreased thoracic drainage-and improves lymph node retrieval for early-stage thymic epithelial tumours. The attenuation of the systemic inflammatory response highlights the biological benefits of robotic precision.Registration number: NCT06654830 (http://www.clinicaltrials.gov).

title: Primary Mediastinal Kaposiform Hemangioendothelioma Involving the Superior Vena Cava in an Adult: An Extremely Rare Entity.
authors: Zhang K, Xin S, Ye Z et al.
abstract: Kaposiform hemangioendothelioma (KHE) is a rare vascular tumour predominantly affecting infants. Primary mediastinal involvement in adults is exceptionally rare. We report a rare adult case mimicking thymoma but involving the superior vena cava (SVC). A 29-year-old male presented with an anterior mediastinal mass suspected as thymoma. Imaging revealed a solid lesion and the patient underwent surgical resection via median sternotomy. Intraoperatively, the tumour showed dense adherence to the SVC, necessitating SVC plasty. Histopathology confirmed KHE. The patient recovered uneventfully. Although KHE is primarily a paediatric diagnosis, it must be considered in the differential diagnosis of adult anterior mediastinal masses. Complete surgical resection remains the treatment of choice, though vascular reconstruction may be required due to the tumour's infiltrative nature.

title: Perioperative immune optimization and surgical readiness in thymoma-associated myasthenia gravis: current evidence and emerging strategies.
authors: Wang L, Wang Z, Feng Y
abstract: Thymoma-associated myasthenia gravis (TAMG) complicates perioperative management because neurological vulnerability must be weighed against the physiological demands of tumor resection. This review examines operation-specific assessment and rapid immune optimization, compares established treatments with emerging neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn) inhibition, and proposes a dual-axis framework integrating myasthenia gravis (MG)-related vulnerability and anticipated operative burden. Intravenous immunoglobulin and plasma exchange remain the established rapid-treatment options when clinically meaningful improvement is needed before surgery. FcRn inhibition provides a mechanistically distinct means of lowering circulating immunoglobulin G. Among FcRn inhibitors, efgartigimod has the most direct perioperative evidence in TAMG, but available studies are small, nonrandomized, and largely confined to selected adults with acetylcholine receptor antibody-positive disease undergoing planned surgery. No randomized trial or TAMG-specific active-comparator study has demonstrated that perioperative efgartigimod reduces postoperative myasthenic crisis or other surgical complications. Its optimal preoperative schedule and the value of routine postoperative continuation remain uncertain. Decisions about rapid immune optimization should consider the recent MG trajectory, bulbar and respiratory function, secretion clearance, operative demands, and available postoperative support. Surgical readiness requires multidisciplinary judgment tailored to the planned operation; it cannot be determined by a single clinical score, antibody level, or predetermined treatment course. The proposed dual-axis framework is intended to structure this discussion but has not been validated.

title: Diagnostic Utility of Transbronchial Mediastinal Cryobiopsy: The First Single-Tertiary Center Experience in Korea.
authors: Kim MJ, Jang YS, Jang S et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Transbronchial mediastinal cryobiopsy (TBMC) is a safe, effective technique that offers higher diagnostic yield for mediastinal lesions-especially lymphoproliferative and nonneoplastic diseases-compared to endobronchial ultrasound (EBUS)-guided transbronchial needle aspiration (TBNA). However, real-world data are limited, particularly in Asian populations. Therefore, this study aimed to compare the diagnostic performance and safety of EBUS-TBNA and TBMC.
METHODS: In this single-center retrospective study in Seoul, Korea, TBMC was used for patients with mediastinal lesions exhibiting imaging features suggestive of non-lung cancer diagnoses, extensive necrosis likely to lower needle-sampling yield, or previous nondiagnostic procedures. Between June 2023 and February 2024, 29 patients underwent TBNA followed by TBMC during EBUS.
RESULTS: The mean age was 59.6 years, and 69% were male. TBNA and TBMC were performed 2.82 and 2.55 times per lesion on average, respectively. Twelve patients had nonneoplastic (e.g., sarcoidosis, tuberculosis, immunoglobulin G4-related disease), and 17 had neoplastic (lung cancer, lymphoma, thymoma) diseases. Adequate tissue was obtained in all transbronchial mediastinal cryobiopsy cases, which showed a significantly higher overall diagnostic yield than TBNA (89.7% vs. 58.6%, P = 0.006), particularly in lymphoma (100% vs. 37.5%, P = 0.025), with no significant difference in lung cancer or nonneoplastic diseases. Mild-to-moderate bleeding occurred in two patients (6.8%) per group and was controlled without complications.
CONCLUSION: Transbronchial mediastinal cryobiopsy demonstrated a higher diagnostic yield than EBUS-TBNA-particularly for lymphoma-with a favorable safety profile.

title: Results reporting and primary endpoint achievement in interventional therapeutic trials for pleural mesothelioma, 2005-2025: a cross-sectional analysis.
authors: Li N, Chen W, Fan S et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pleural mesothelioma (PM) is a rare and aggressive malignancy in which therapeutic progress depends on a limited clinical trial evidence base. Although trial registration has improved transparency, the extent to which registered trials generate publicly available and clinically interpretable evidence remains unclear. We evaluated results reporting, primary endpoint achievement, and trial characteristics according to reporting status in registered interventional therapeutic trials for PM.
METHODS: We conducted a cross-sectional analysis of registered interventional therapeutic trials for PM on ClinicalTrials.gov from 2005 to 2025. Trial characteristics, completion status, public results reporting, and whether the prespecified primary endpoint was met were abstracted from ClinicalTrials.gov and complementary public sources. Reporting and primary-endpoint analyses included trials with a primary completion date at least 12 months before data abstraction. Trials were considered reported if results were publicly available from any source. Primary endpoint achievement was defined according to whether the prespecified primary endpoint was reported as met, without reclassification based on perceived clinical relevance or secondary outcomes. Trial characteristics were compared descriptively according to reporting status using Fisher exact tests.
RESULTS: We identified 150 interventional therapeutic trials, representing a planned cumulative enrollment of 12,406 participants. Immunotherapy-containing strategies increased from 2.7% of trials in 2005-2015 to 39.5% in 2016-2025. Among 114 trials that had reached primary completion, 28 (24.6%) had no publicly available results. In descriptive comparisons, nonreporting was more frequent among trials with planned enrollment below 50 participants and among nonrandomized studies. Among 86 trials with reported results, the prespecified primary endpoint was met in 33 (38.4%), not met in 41 (47.7%), and not evaluable in 12 (14.0%). Among randomized trials with classifiable primary-endpoint status, 9 of 27 (33.3%) met their prespecified primary endpoint.
CONCLUSIONS: Registered interventional therapeutic trials for PM have increasingly shifted toward immunotherapy-containing strategies; however, incomplete public reporting and the limited proportion of reported randomized trials with classifiable outcomes that met their prespecified primary endpoints constrain clinical interpretation.

title: Multi-Omics Profiling Reveals NF2 Loss-Driven Glycosphingolipid Remodeling in Mesothelial Cells.
authors: Sato T, Kano K, Kondo-Ida L et al.
abstract: Neurofibromin 2 (NF2) loss is common in malignant mesothelioma and is associated with the activation of Yes-associated protein/transcriptional co-activator with PDZ-binding motif (YAP/TAZ)-dependent transcription. However, its effects on cellular lipid metabolism remain unclear. In this study, we integrated non-targeted lipidomics with transcriptomic and proteomic analyses of MeT-5A mesothelial cells to characterize NF2 deficiency-induced lipid metabolic remodeling. NF2 loss was associated with significant accumulation of glycosylated ceramides, particularly hexosylceramides, accompanied by increased UDP-glucose ceramide glucosyltransferase (UGCG) expression. Analysis of public transcriptomic datasets revealed that UGCG expression was positively associated with YAP/TAZ-TEA domain transcription factor activity in mesothelial and mesothelioma cells and was associated with poorer clinical outcomes in patients with mesothelioma. Pharmacological inhibition of UGCG using miglustat reduced hexosylceramide levels and was accompanied by increased sphingomyelin (SM) levels. Although inhibiting either ceramide glycosylation or SM synthesis alone had limited effects on cell growth, their combined inhibition using miglustat and malabaricone C markedly suppressed cell growth in both parental and NF2-deficient MeT-5A cells. Together, these findings identify NF2 loss-associated glycosphingolipid remodeling as a previously unrecognized metabolic feature of mesothelial cells.

title: DNA Methyltransferase Inhibition During CAR T-cell Manufacturing Enhances Antitumor Activity in Immunocompetent Brain and Ovarian Cancer Models
summary: Limited persistence and progressive dysfunction remain major barriers to effective CAR T-cell therapy for solid tumors. Epigenetic regulation, particularly DNA methylation, can reinforce dysfunctional T-cell programs by restricting expression of genes required for sustained effector function. CAR T-cell manufacturing provides an opportunity to pharmacologically prime CAR T-cells prior to infusion without additional treatment burden. Therefore, we hypothesized that transient DNA methyltransferase (DNMT) inhibition during CAR T-cell manufacturing would epigenetically modulate CAR T-cell state and enhance functional and antitumor activity against solid tumors. We evaluated transient DNMT inhibition during ex vivo murine CAR T-cell manufacturing using two mechanistically distinct compounds: the nucleoside analogue 5-azacytidine (5-Aza) and the selective DNMT1 inhibitor GSK3685032 (GSK). Epigenetic and transcriptomic profiling, together with functional analyses including repeated antigen stimulation, were performed to characterize the molecular and functional effects of DNMT inhibition on CAR T-cells. Therapeutic efficacy was evaluated in immunocompetent syngeneic murine models of pediatric glioma and ovarian cancer by assessing tumor burden and survival. 5-Aza treatment induced dose-dependent epigenetic and transcriptional changes in CAR T-cells that were accompanied by enhanced expansion, sustained cytotoxicity and cytokine production during repeated antigen challenge in vitro. These improvements translated in vivo, with enhanced tumor control across immunocompetent models of high-grade glioma, diffuse midline glioma, and ovarian cancer using both B7-H3- and GD2-targeting CAR constructs. The dose associated with the greatest benefit varied by CAR construct and tumor model. In contrast, selective DNMT1 inhibition with GSK did not recapitulate the molecular or functional benefits of 5-Aza and reduced therapeutic efficacy in vivo. Collectively, these findings demonstrate
